A Latch-On-Resistant, False-Alarm-Gated Lead-Time Metric for Bearing Anomaly Detection — and What It Reveals About SCADA-Rate Logging Ansh Goyal1 1 Jaypee Institute of Information Technology, Noida, India anshgoyal500@gmail.com ABSTRACT Anomaly detectors for rolling-element-bearing prognostics are typically evaluated by classification accuracy, which answers whether a fault is detected but not how early or at what false-alarm cost.

We argue that lead time, the warning interval before failure, is the operationally decisive quantity, and we make it the primary evaluation object through a latch-on-resistant, false-alarm-gated metric.
Warning time is credited only when the pre-onset false-alarm rate lies within a stated budget τ , so a degenerate constant-on detector is provably scored invalid.
We then ask whether the bin-averaged logging of a SCADA historian destroys detection lead time relative to simple decimation.

Condition-based maintenance (CBM) and prognostics and health management (PHM) promise to replace fixed-interval servicing with data-driven intervention, reducing both unplanned downtime and unnecessary maintenance (Jardine, Lin, & Banjevic, 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018).

Rolling-element bearings are the most common failure mode in rotating machinery, and a large literature applies statistical control charts, classical machine learning, and deep models to detect incipient bearing faults from vibration (Randall & Antoni, 2011; Zhao et al., 2019).

The economic case is well established: a warning delivered hours or days before a catastrophic seizure lets an operator schedule an orderly shutdown, order parts, and avoid secondary damage to shafts, housings, and couplings.
Despite this, most published detectors are evaluated with classification metrics—accuracy, precision/recall, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC- AUC).
These answer “was the failure detected?” but not the question a maintenance planner actually asks: “how many hours of warning did we get, and how often did the system cry wolf?
A detector that warns 48 h ahead at a low nuisance-alarm rate is operationally distinct from one that fires minutes before breakdown or one that alarms every day.

The prognostics community has long advocated time-aware metrics (Saxena et al., 2008; Saxena, Celaya, Saha, Saha, & Goebel, 2010; Goebel, Saha, & Saxena, 2011), yet lead time is rarely the headline quantity in detector benchmarks, and ad hoc lead-time definitions are easy to game.

In particular, any lead-time metric that does not pair warning time with a false-alarm constraint can be trivially maximized by a detector that simply alarms from the first sample—a “latch-on” exploit that earns the full run length as lead time while being operationally useless.
A second, eminently practical question motivates this study.

Industrial Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) historians rarely store raw high-rate vibration; they store decimated or time-averaged summaries at a coarse logging interval (Tautz-Weinert & Watson, 2017)—seconds to minutes, rather than the tens of kilohertz at which accelerometers are sampled.

The folklore concern is that this storage step destroys fault-relevant information: that bin-averaging the summary statistics a historian retains washes out the very excursions that signal an incipient spall, so that the act of long-term storage would blind any prognostic algorithm that consumes the historian.
Whether this is actually true is an empirical question that, to our knowledge, has not been tested with a sound lead-time metric across multiple datasets.

The answer matters: if averaging is harmless, operators can store compact, cheap, bin-averaged streams without sacrificing warning time; if it is harmful, the implication is that prognostics-grade monitoring requires separate high-rate acquisition.
This paper makes both questions precise and answers them.

Scope of claims.
The empirical results are for rollingelement bearings under approximately steady operating conditions; we make no claim of transfer to gearboxes, blades, or variable-speed machinery.
The sampling question is specifically bin-averaged historian storage versus decimated storage.
The metric itself is failure-mode-agnostic: it applies wherever a run-to-failure trajectory and a stationary normal region exist.
We deliberately report a result that is not the one we set out to find.
Our working hypothesis was that bin-averaging the stored summary series would wash out incipient-fault excursions and shorten lead time.
It does not.
We regard reporting the refutation, with its dataset-dependent direction made explicit, as more valuable than a tidy but unsupported positive claim.

Reviews of machinery diagnostics and prognostics (Jardine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018) and of remaininguseful-life (RUL) estimation (Si, Wang, Hu, & Zhou, 2011) establish the CBM/PHM framing in which a health indicator is tracked and an alarm or RUL estimate is produced.
Saxena et al.
(2008), Saxena et al.
(2010), and Goebel et al.
(2011) propose a family of prognostic-performance metrics (prognostic horizon, α-λ accuracy, relative accuracy, and timeliness) that explicitly reward early, well-calibrated predictions.
Our onset-relative lead time is in this spirit: it measures warning time relative to a degradation event rather than to an arbitrary positional marker.

We depart from prior practice in one key respect: we make the false-alarm budget an integral part of the metric’s validity condition rather than a separately reported number, which is precisely what closes the latch-on loophole.

We further provide, to our knowledge, the first formal comparison showing that an ungated prognostic-horizon metric produces a different and operationally misleading detector ranking relative to a false-alarm-budgeted metric (Section 6.11, Table 15).

The disagreement is not marginal: on IMS the detectors the prognostic horizon ranks first by raw lead (Hotelling T 2, Isolation Forest, and EWMA) each have no valid operating point at a 10% false-alarm budget, while our metric identifies 3σ as the deployable choice.

The cost asymmetry between a missed detection and a false alarm has been treated explicitly outside bearing prognostics.

The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (Lavin & Ahmad, 2015) scores streaming detectors under an application profile that rewards early detection and penalises false positives, making the same commitment our gate makes in a different domain: that earliness cannot be assessed independently of nuisancealarm behaviour.
The difference is structural.

That benchmark folds both into a single weighted score, so a detector may trade false alarms against earliness and still rank well; our budget is a validity condition, and an alarm outside it earns no credit that a longer lead can offset.
A parallel line of work revises evaluation itself for time-series detection.

Tatbul, Lee, Zdonik, Alam, and Gottschlich (2018) generalise precision and recall from points to ranges with a tunable positional bias, so that early detection within an anomalous interval can be rewarded explicitly, and Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that widely used benchmarks admit trivial solutions and overstate progress.

Our metric shares the diagnosis and differs in what it reports: rather than a score on a bounded scale, the gated lead time is a physical quantity— hours of warning—that a maintenance planner can act on directly, and the false-alarm constraint enters as a gate on validity rather than as a weight inside the score.

Univariate and multivariate statistical-process-control charts—the 3σ rule, the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) (Roberts, 1959), and Hotelling’s T 2 (Hotelling, 1947)—remain workhorses of industrial monitoring (Montgomery, 2009) because they are interpretable and require little training data.

In the unsupervised machinelearning family, Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting, & Zhou, 2008) and the one-class support vector machine (SVM) (Schölkopf, Platt, Shawe-Taylor, Smola, & Williamson, 2001) are widely deployed; deep models such as LSTM autoencoders (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Malhotra et al., 2016; Hundman, Constantinou, Laporte, Colwell, & Soderstrom, 2018) and Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) have been applied to machine-health monitoring (Zhao et al., 2019).

We evaluate representatives of both the classical and learning families under a single, fixed hyperparameter protocol so that the comparison is about the evaluation and the sampling question, not about detector tuning.
Relation to published FEMTO/XJTU results.

The FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY campaigns are best known through the IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and subsequent remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012), whose leading methods report a RUL-error score on the deliberately truncated Test/Validation copies of the bearings.

The FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY campaigns are best known through the IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and subsequent remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012), whose leading methods report a RUL-error score on the deliberately truncated Test/Validation copies of the bearings.

Those numbers are not directly comparable to ours for two structural reasons: (i) they estimate a continuous RUL on runs with no observed failure, whereas our metric measures early-warning lead time on the complete run-to-failure trajectory and gates it on a pre-onset false-alarm budget; and (ii) they do not report a false-alarm rate at all, so a method’s RUL score says nothing about whether its alarm would survive our τ gate—the very quantity we argue is decisive.
We therefore do not tabulate their RUL scores against our lead times, which would be a category error.

The classic normalized-RMS health-indicator with a first-prediction-time threshold—the workhorse baseline underlying most of that literature—is represented here by our rms_trend detector, evaluated under the same gated metric as every other method; re-evaluating specific published architectures under the gated metric (which requires their original code) is left as future work.
The pairing of detection delay with a false-alarm constraint is the founding formulation of sequential change detection.

Lorden (1971) posed the minimax problem of minimising worst-case detection delay subject to a lower bound on the average run length to false alarm, and Moustakides (1986) later showed that the cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart of Page (1954) is exactly optimal under that criterion; Pollak (1985) gives the corresponding result for a revised delay measure.

Our gate inherits the same premise and applies it at a different stage: that theory constrains the false-alarm rate when a detector is designed, by choosing a threshold that meets a stated run-length bound, whereas we impose it when a detector is scored, against a rate measured on the data.
The two can disagree.

Uncertainty Quantification and Conformal Prediction
Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005; Laxhammar & Falkman, 2014) provides a distribution-free guarantee that the false-alarm rate is bounded by a target α under exchangeability.
This is attractive for prognostics because it converts a detector’s raw score into an alarm with an interpretable, finite-sample false-alarm guarantee.

We wire conformal calibration into the lead-time pipeline and, rather than assuming the guarantee, test it empirically across runs— including a run where exchangeability provably fails because the “normal” region already contains degradation.
Bearing-defect frequencies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006), and envelope (demodulation) analysis (Randall & Antoni, 2011) are the classical frequency-domain tools for bearing diagnostics.

We include fast Fourier transform (FFT) band energies, spectral kurtosis, and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies, and we ablate them against pure time-domain statistics to see which family actually carries prognostic lead time under our gated metric.

Tautz-Weinert and Watson (2017) review SCADA-data condition monitoring and note explicitly that historian aggregation is a recognized but under-quantified concern: practitioners suspect that coarse averaging hurts fault detection, but the magnitude of the effect has not been measured with a principled warning-time metric.
The present paper addresses exactly this gap, and reaches the perhaps surprising conclusion that, for bearing faults, the concern is not borne out.

Algorithm 1 Leakage-free terminal degradation onset The terminal-excursion rule has a predictable bias.

The onset fires at the first sample of the last sustained excursion above the band β = µb + kσb, so for a degradation ramp of slope m the estimator is late by approximately kσb/m, with a standard deviation of order σb/m.

The persistence requirement P does not enter this bias: Algorithm 1 returns min Rlast, the start of the qualifying run, so P governs which excursions are admitted rather than delaying the timestamp reported for an admitted one.

Both bias and spread scale inversely with the ramp slope: the estimator is near-unbiased and stable under abrupt degradation, where the delay falls to the sampling interval ∆t alone, and systematically late and more variable under gradual degradation.

Four methodological corrections, applied together, change the conclusion of the sampling study.
First, a correct failure label for the third IMS test (which had left a fifth of the data after the nominal failure) turns a guaranteed miss into a valid detection.
Second, an onset-gated metric that defeats the latch-on exploit prevents a constant-on detector from manufacturing lead time.
Third, a p < n, channel-invariant feature space removes the ill-posedness of a channel-countdependent scheme.
Fourth, a statistical test on the genuine unit of inference—the run, not the within-run sampling factor—replaces an eyeballed curve and a pseudoreplicated paired test.

With all four in place, the original claim that SCADA averaging destroys lead time is refuted on every dataset tested, and the previously-reported significant positive effect is corrected to a consistent but non-significant trend.
